entry.title: Weight Space Misfolding
$11.4M in Nvidia hardware vanishes during shipment from CA to TX
entry.content:
Six pallets of NVIDIA computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million disappeared during a shipment from California to Texas. A truck collected the merchandise in Oakland on Aug. 29 for delivery to Fort Worth. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through several extended stops before losing its trail in Southern California. The Oakland Police Department confirmed an ongoing grand theft investigation following a complaint filed Sept. 13, 2026. The disappearance comes amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data center freight involving other high-value technology shipments.

According to The Mercury News, the vehicle displayed a food transportation company’s logo during the scheduled pickup. The driver subsequently traveled south, making several stops lasting multiple hours. Investigators eventually lost track of the truck in San Bernardino County. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation involved suspects who allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight. Authorities have not linked the two investigations.

Oakland police confirm investigation

The Oakland Police Department provided FreightWaves with the following statement:

“The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026. The investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact the OPD General Crimes Unit at (510) 238-3728.”

The Sept. 13 complaint date does not establish when the theft occurred. Police have not confirmed the reported $11.4 million valuation or identified the specific merchandise. Authorities also have not identified the cargo’s owner, shipper, motor carrier or driver. Investigators have not publicly explained the vehicle’s extended stops or established whether criminals impersonated a transportation provider. Police have not announced arrests or confirmed any recovery of the merchandise. FreightWaves contacted NVIDIA for comment and followed up, but the company has not responded.

Previous thefts involving NVIDIA products

The Oakland investigation follows other significant thefts involving NVIDIA merchandise in Northern California. During 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA products. Those incidents targeted valuable computer hardware at separate locations. Authorities have not established any connection between those investigations and the latest disappearance.

In a separate September incident, thieves stole two PlusAI trailers, including one displaying NVIDIA branding, from a Fremont, California, warehouse. The trailers contained approximately 40,000 pounds of sand rather than NVIDIA hardware. Police recovered both trailers in nearby Newark. Investigators have not established any connection between that theft and the Oakland case.

Why it matters

The reported disappearance of $11.4 million in NVIDIA hardware underscores the financial stakes of transporting high-value freight. Regardless of how this shipment disappeared, carrier verification, shipment visibility and communication remain critical throughout transportation.Click here for more articles on cargo theft and freight fraud by Phil Brink.

entry.title: Perplexity Decider v1.3: Training, eval, and use cases
entry.content:
Perplexity Decider

How we train, evaluate, and use it.

We are releasing Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, the successors to our earlier decision models: v1, v1.1, v1.2, and Flash v1.2.

Decider Flash v1.3 is a smaller model distilled from Decider v1.3. Both models are available on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.

Perplexity Decider is inspired by Jev, TypeSafe AIâs System One Model. It supports binary and multi-class classification with ordered or unordered labels, returning probabilities that applications can use to classify, route, rank, and evaluate inputs.

Both v1.3 models improve performance and robustness across a broad range of text and vision tasks through bidirectional attention, better-curated training data, and a refined training recipe. We also introduce locate, a new feature to highlight the selected content for named entity recognition, personal information identification, and extractive question-answering tasks.

In this post, we explain how we train and evaluate Decider and share how we use it internally at Perplexity.

What is a decision model?

A decision model is a general-purpose classifier. You give it an input and a set of questions each with its possible answers. For each question, it returns a probability distribution over the answers. It supports 3 question types:

Yes / No: binary decisions. Multiple choice: custom multi-class labels. Score: ordered levels.

Decision models support a wide range of classification and scoring tasks:

Judging outputs: assessing faithfulness, quality, and safety. Routing: directing requests to smaller or larger models based on difficulty. Moderation and security: detecting harmful content, phishing, and prompt injection in tool outputs. Filtering and tagging: organizing large collections of content. Retrieval and reranking: scoring search results by relevance.

Many of these tasks were previously handled by generative models like LLMs, even though they do not require free-form text generation. Decision models sit between LLMs and task-specific classifiers. They return probabilities for multiple questions about the same input in a single forward pass, avoiding token-by-token answer generation and sharing computation across questions. Unlike task-specific classifiers, they can handle new tasks through natural language prompts, a flexibility learned from training across diverse tasks in a shared question-answering format.

Training Turning a generative LLM into a decision model

We build Decider by adapting strong generative LLM backbones. To explain the adaptation, we first describe how a request is represented. As illustrated below, a request consists out of a shared context (the state) and a number of questions. The state will be reused by all questions.

For example, given a document and its summary, a single request can ask whether the summary faithfully represents the document and whether it is intended for an expert or a general audience. After the state, each question block contains a question and its possible answers, each assigned a predefined label token such as A, B, or C. A special <|marker|> token indicates where to read out the modelâs prediction. At this position, a learned linear output layer (a decision head), maps the hidden state to scores for the questionâs answer options, which are then converted to probabilities.

We initialize the output layer from the base model, which normally scores next-token from the entire vocabulary, and only keep the rows corresponding to the predefined option tokens such as A, B, or C. This pruned layer is then trained to turn the hidden state of <|marker|> into answer scores. This approach covers all classification questions because they can all be formulated as a multiple choice.

For training, we take hundreds of public datasets spanning diverse tasks (sentiment, natural language inference, intent detection, entity matching, moderation, fact checking, ratings, etc.) and convert each example into the unified format described above: a state, one or more questions, their options and a target. The target can be the single correct option if we have gold labels, or a probability distribution over options.

In v1.3, we introduce locate, which extracts text from the state instead of selecting from predefined options. A locate question describes what to find, using either a short label such as âlocationâ or an instruction such as âExtract the city name where the job is located.â The model returns the exact matching text from the state, along with its start and end character locations. If it identifies no matches, it returns an empty list.

Because of shared state, a single request can combine locate, classification, and scoring questions about the same input. For example, it can ask whether a job requires senior-level experience and extract the required skills.

Bidirectional attention: letting the model read both ways

Our models start from strong pretrained generative backbones, whose causal attention lets each token attend only to itself and preceding tokens. Our ablation studies showed that making the backboneâs full-attention layers bidirectional improves performance, so we adopt this design to let each token incorporate context from the entire input.

Bidirectional attention introduces another design choice: how should the state and questions interact? We considered three attention patterns, with different implications for performance, answer stability, and cache reuse:

Everything sees everything (v1.2): The state and all questions are processed together with full bidirectional attention. Computation over the state is shared, but an answer to one question can change depending on what else is asked. Isolated questions (v1.3): The state attends to all the questions, while each question attends only to the state and its own tokens. Questions can still influence one another indirectly through the shared state but results are more stable. Fully cacheable: The state only attends to itself, while each question attends to the state and its own tokens. The state is question-independent and reusable across requests to take advantage of prompt caching. We don't use it by default, because letting the state see the questions matters a lot for several tasks, but a small fine-tuning can switch a model to it.

We ultimately chose isolated questions for their strong performance and stability.

Training recipe

Training proceeds in three stages for both model sizes. We first train the larger model, based on Qwen3.8-27B, using cross-entropy on large datasets, then distill it into the smaller Qwen3.5-4B model.

The first stage is generalist training, where we fully fine-tune the model on large-scale corpora. In this stage, we only accept data that helps the model across the board and is not specific to any benchmark; we thus exclude any benchmark training splits.

After this generalist model is trained, we run a second, more fine-grained stage using LoRA. The data used in this stage is targeted toward specific domains and tasks. We add data in the second stage rather than the first one if we observe narrow gains or if we observe some regressions on other tasks. We use LoRA to avoid drifting too much from the generalist model and risking losing performance to fit those specific domains. The goal is to improve performance while retaining the backboneâs general knowledge. We also use a weight when merging the LoRA back into the base model, to control the drift more precisely and favor held-out metrics above any in-domain gains.

Finally, we add a vision-specific step. Similar to the second stage, the vision step is treated as another fine-grained specialization step, using a LoRA adapter that is merged back to the base model with a weight. Some vision capabilities can come at the price of text performance. Since we observe much more usage of the models on text, we prioritize text metrics over vision metrics.

For both text stages, we use the average weights from three runs, each using a different random seed. We found this improves the performance and robustness of the aggregated model.

Once the final large model is obtained, we apply the same three-stage training procedure to the smaller model. Here, the large model acts as the teacher: its predicted output distribution replaces the gold labels, and the smaller model is trained to minimize the KL divergence between its predictions and those of the teacher. This distillation objective outperforms cross-entropy on the same training data. While cross-entropy performs better on benchmarks with dedicated training data, it generalizes less well to held-out data. We hypothesize that distillation better transfers the teacherâs output distribution, including its confidence over non-gold alternatives, whereas cross-entropy encourages overfitting to the benchmark-specific training distribution. We therefore adopt the KL-based distillation objective.

To mitigate train-test contamination, we remove any training samples that could overlap with any evaluation we use. This is important because some public training datasets contain large parts of some evaluation datasets. We also conduct extensive bias audits and removal to make sure our gains are reliable and not just driven by learned biases.

Adding the ability to extract information

The locate feature extracts information such as named entities from text, without changing how it answers ordinary requests. To do so, we introduce an additional training stage: we add a new special token, <|locate|>, a span head, and LoRA adapter to Decider.

We initialize <|locate|> âs embedding from <|marker|> learned in the previous training stages. We train only this new embedding, the span head, and the LoRA adapters, while keeping the original backbone weights and decision head frozen. Each requested field gets its own <|locate|> token.

The span head uses <|locate|> âs representation together with the state-token representations to score where matching spans start and end, and which start-end pairs belong together. It also uses the <|locate|> tokenâs representation to predict field-specific thresholds for these scores. Selected spans are returned as character positions in the original text.

We train the span head with an adapted InfoNCE loss that pushes every gold span above the threshold, and the threshold above every other span. The loss has two terms: The first one pushes the scores of correct spans above the threshold and the wrong spans. The second term pushes the threshold above the scores of wrong spans. Fields with no answer get only the second term, which teaches the model to return an empty list.

We train on a mix of span extraction tasks, including named entity recognition, PII detection and extractive question answering. We vary the field descriptions from short labels to detailed instructions, so the model learns to follow the request rather than memorize a fixed label set.

Locate teaches the model a structurally different task, and we want to add it without losing what the model already does well. Merging the locate adapters into the backbone causes some regression on decision requests. To limit this, we are running investigations such as more replay data from earlier stages and auxiliary objectives that keep the modelâs outputs on decision requests close to those of the original model. However, we find that merging is currently still not lossless, so we keep the adapters unmerged and activate them only for locate requests.

Evaluation

We evaluate Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 on external benchmarks from the Hugging Face Decision Index, Vals AIâs ClaimBench, and Artificial Analysis Decision Index.

Across these evaluations, our models demonstrate strong performance. Even though these leaderboards include privately held tasks, they can still be gamed through repeated submission and iterative tuning based on leaderboard feedback. To complement these leaderboards, we evaluate the models on an internal suite combining private production tasks with held-out evaluations drawn from public non-benchmark datasets. These evaluations provide an additional check on generalization beyond public benchmarks, helping us distinguish broader improvements from gains specific to familiar evaluation suites.

Internally, we built a suite of more than 200 tasks spanning various domains and tasks such as classification, scoring, reranking, and entity extraction. To honestly assess Deciderâs real-world performance, all evaluations are performed zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, giving us a clear signal of where to improve the model.

Query classification

At Perplexity, we use a multi-head classification system to process each user query. Each query is first passed through an embedding model that acts as a feature extractor. The resulting embedding is then fed into multiple separate classification heads, including both binary and multi-label classifiers. For example, one head determines whether a user query should trigger web search.

Across 63 classification tasks with independently relabeled references by a frontier LLM, Decider v1.3 achieves 91.6% mean accuracy, exceeding our production classifiers by 6.54 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 also outperforms the production baseline, while Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14.

Domain-specific classification

We assembled a domain-specific evaluation suite from public datasets to assess decision modelsâ classification performance across seven domains: claim verification (6 tasks), healthcare (7), cybersecurity (8), programming (16), government (7), law (9) and finance (9).

For example, âjudge the time complexity of a Python programâ, or âuse an annual financial report to determine whether a companyâs unrestricted cash covers debt principal due within the next twelve monthsâ. Decider v1.3 leads across all seven domains, outperforming Jev 1.14 by up to 12.9 percentage points in finance and 9.3 points in law. Decider Flash v1.3 trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming, and law, and performs similarly in other domains.

Retrieval and Reranking

Search is at the core of Perplexity. We maintain a broad suite of retrieval tasks to evaluate our modelsâ reranking performance. For each task, we first use a pool of embedding models to retrieve the top 50 candidate documents from each corpus. We then rerank these candidates using Decider and compare its performance against a strong reranker baseline, Qwen3-Reranker-8B.

We evaluate Decider in a zero-shot, pointwise setting, using the model to directly score each queryâdocument pair independently and rank documents by relevance. Across 72 retrieval tasks, Decider v1.3 achieves a mean nDCG@10 of 83.99, outperforming Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 1.81 points and Jev 1.14 by 2.24 points.

On the BEIR benchmark, both models outperform Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 8.78 and 7.05 nDCG@10 respectively. Against Jev 1.14, Decider v1.3 is 1.33 points higher, while the Flash version scores 0.4 lower.

Multilingual classification

To evaluate decision models beyond English, we assembled a multilingual classification benchmark comprising 19 language-specific tasks from 8 public datasets, with 46,484 examples across eight languages: German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. The benchmark covers intent detection, topic classification, sentiment analysis, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, offensive language detection, and grammatical acceptability.

We report mean accuracy across tasks within each language, weighting each task equally. Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14 in all eight languages and Decider Flash v1.3 does so in six, with mean task accuracies of 88.16% for Decider v1.3 and 86.50% for Decider Flash v1.3, compared with 85.41% for Jev 1.14.

NER, PII and Extractive QA

We evaluate the locate feature on 17 out-of-domain tasks that test its extraction across various domains, input formats (text, tables, structured documents) and instructions (short labels, questions and detailed descriptions). The domains range from Wikipedia to scientific papers, cyber-threat reports, technical support, privacy policies, resumes, and legal contracts. The requests range from short label names such as âpersonâ or âemail addressâ, through questions about a table or a support ticket, to detailed field descriptions for structured extraction, such as the parties of an NDA or the total on an invoice.

We evaluate NER and PII using exact-span F1, which requires predicted spans to match the reference boundaries exactly. Extractive QA uses character-level F1, giving partial credit for overlapping answer text, while structured extraction uses field accuracy, the proportion of fields extracted correctly. For CV parsing, we average the NER and PII exact-span F1 scores.

We compare our models against general-purpose extraction models of different sizes: GLiNER large v2.5 (0.5B), Liquid d1 (2B) and Cloudflareâs Clairic (undisclosed). Decider v1.3 reaches an average score of 69.0 (using each taskâs primary metric) and Decider Flash v1.3 reaches 63.6, compared with 43.3 for Liquid d1, 41.5 for Clairic and 33.6 for GLiNER large v2.5. Both Decider models lead in every category.

Image classification

Decider has natively supported vision tasks since v1. To evaluate its performance beyond text, we assembled a five-task benchmark suite with a particular focus on document classification, including invoices, letters, and resumes. The suite also covers satellite image classification, texture classification, pet breed classification, and animal counting.

Decider v1.3 achieves a mean accuracy of 76.99% across the five visual tasks, outperforming Jev 1.14 by 1.47 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 achieves 72.77%, demonstrating visual classification capabilities in a smaller model.

Real-world decision requests

We sampled one million deduplicated, PII-masked requests submitted to the Perplexity Decision API during its first 18 days of availability. Because each request can contain multiple questions about the same state, the sample comprises 2,318,887 individual questions. All requests were included with explicit user permission for research.

Production requests do not come with ground-truth labels, so we use frontier LLM judges to generate reference answers and measure each modelâs agreement with them. We also group the requests into 10 task categories, including information extraction, domain classification, sentiment analysis, intent and routing, relevance ranking, content moderation, quality and compliance review, entity matching, business analysis, and an âOtherâ category. This breakdown shows how performance varies across real-world use cases.

The task mix is uneven: information extraction accounts for 425,402 questions, domain classification for 409,564, and sentiment analysis for 344,158. Together, these three categories make up 50.8% of the sampled questions.

Decider v1.3 achieves the highest agreement with the judges at 93.98%, compared with 93.68% for Decider v1.2 and 93.35% for Jev 1.14. Decider v1.3 and Jev 1.14 are closely matched on domain classification and sentiment analysis, with gaps of 0.34 and 0.07 percentage points, respectively. Jev leads by 0.69 points on relevance ranking, while Decider v1.3 leads by 0.93 points on information extraction (the most common task in the sample) and by 1.21 points on intent and routing.

The chart below compares the reported cost of running the same one million production requests. Each request can contain multiple questions, so the unit here is requests, not individual questions.

Robustness

We evaluated label sensitivity on 372 multiple-choice questions, making 4,788 requests per model. We reordered options, reassigned labels to answer texts, and renamed labels while preserving each questionâs meaning, then checked whether the modelâs semantic answer changed. Lower flip rates indicate greater stability.

Decider v1.3 changed its answer on just 0.27% of questions under each transformation, compared with 2.69â4.84% for Jev 1.14. We also repeated identical inputs to measure serving variability: Decider v1.3 showed no changes, while Jev 1.14 changed on 1.88% of questions.

How we use Decider

Decider is built for workflows that need fast and structured decisions. In this section we explore how to leverage them to produce meaningful impact on the way we work. Here are some that stood out.

Self-improving security rules

Internally, we are already using Decider to improve our security policies.

The activity of our agents is recorded and a series of rule-based checks are performed to identify any problematic behavior. A rule-based approach means that we can monitor our agents in real-time with negligible latency added. Offline, we use Decider to look at samples from these recorded agent logs. In the case that no problematic behavior was flagged, Decider checks if there is something that our set of rules missed; and in the case that an alarm was raised, Decider checks whether this was a false alarm. Any records where our rule set fails in either case are sent to an agent for triage and a fix to the rules is proposed, to be approved by a member of our security team.

In one day, Decider read 1 billion tokens across 7,000 agent sessions and identified flaws that led to 14 rule fixes, 6 of which were approved and shipped within two days. Replayed on a week of logs, the fixes cut our busiest rule's volume by 52%, and the widened rules caught about 40% more legitimate actions to investigate.

Monitoring RL rollouts

When we post-train models with reinforcement learning, aggregate metrics such as a terminal reward do not explain why a rollout (an individual attempt at a task) succeeded or failed. It can lose reward unfairly because a tool service or the sandbox failed, or receive undeserved reward if the evaluator overlooks an unsupported claim, such as a made-up value that no tool returned.

We use Decider to monitor rollouts for these cases. Code first identifies parts of a rollout that warrant closer inspection: a failed tool call and the surrounding reasoning, code that ran without errors, or the final answer. Decider then answers multiple-choice questions about each part, such as what failed in a step (a tool service, an external site, the sandbox, the harness, or the agentâs own code) and whether the agent interpreted the result correctly. We bundle all questions about a given part into a single request and store the probabilities rather than a verdict, so we can adjust thresholds later without querying Decider again. The monitor only observes and diagnoses: it never changes a reward or stops a run.

Page quality filtering

When crawling web pages to index and serve to users, many pages are too low quality to be of any use. This includes anti-bot walls, CAPTCHAs, and error pages, as well as correctly loaded web pages that just donât contain any helpful information, such as spam, SEO filler or navigation-only pages. These low-quality pages need to be identified and filtered out of our index.

Using Decider, we can judge the quality of pages as we crawl them. In the same forward pass, we perform a suite of other classification tasks such as identifying the domain and intended audience of the content and whether it contains harmful, illegal, or personally identifiable information. Compared to using an LLM judge, Decider is considerably faster and cheaper.

Beyond these internal uses, Decider also fits workflows such as the following.

Visual QA

Because Decider reads images, it also works as a visual checker, reviewing style changes to web pages or apps and identifying faults. It can review page screenshots for clipped text, overlapping elements, broken layouts before a change ships, or flag charts whose design could mislead a reader or break a brand guide.

Browser navigation

Agents can use Decider for the small decisions inside larger tasks. A browser agent can send a screenshot at each step and receive detailed information about the state of the page and the expected outcome of each possible action.

Planning research tasks

Usersâ questions can greatly vary in their complexity, as does the depth of search that needs to be performed to find an answer. Decider can estimate this before search begins, allowing for fewer resources to be spent on simple questions.

Getting started

Decider returns probabilities. The appropriate decision threshold depends on the application. Label frequencies and the relative costs of false positives and false negatives vary across use cases. We therefore encourage users to tune thresholds on a small, representative labeled development set rather than assume that a fixed cutoff will work equally well across tasks.

We recommend using Decider v1.3 for nuanced judgments, detailed rubrics, and workflows where errors are costly. Choose Decider Flash v1.3 for high-volume routing, labeling, and filtering where latency and cost are the main constraints. Evaluate both models on representative examples from your workload, then choose the model that meets your quality, latency, and budget requirements.

Both models are available as downloadable weights on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.

entry.title: Live-migration support in FreeBSD and bhyve coming
entry.content:
This project presents a first working state for live migration of bhyve guests on FreeBSD 15.1. A running amd64 guest can move between two hosts over TCP while continuing to run; it is paused only for the final stop-and-copy phase. The work builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot support and adds dirty-page tracking in the vmm kernel module together with a migration protocol in bhyve and bhyvectl.

I previously discussed the state of bhyve live migration, its historical development, existing limitations, and why it matters for the future of FreeBSD virtualization in my article bhyve on FreeBSD and VM Live Migration – Quo vadis?.

The goal is deliberately practical: make it possible to test, discuss, and improve a real implementation rather than discuss live migration only in the abstract. The current code and test tooling are being published as a WIP RFC so that the next steps can be shaped in the open. A more detailed demonstration of a VM being live migrated can be watched on my YouTube channel.

Why this matters

Live migration is an important building block for enterprise virtualisation. It enables host maintenance, hardware replacement, load balancing, and failure-domain management with far less disruption to workloads. It is also central to the Sylve project, which aims to offer a Proxmox-like virtualisation solution for FreeBSD. Migration is not an optional convenience in that kind of platform; it is one of the capabilities that makes clustered operations practical.

It is equally important for BoxyBSD, where I offer free BSD-based VPS instances to individuals. Without a credible migration path, routine host work can require a guest outage. That makes live migration a current show stopper for the project, and is why this work is being pushed toward a testable, reviewable state.

How the current implementation works

The source starts with a pre-copy phase. It sends populated guest memory, then repeatedly obtains a bitmap of pages changed since the previous scan and sends only those pages. Once the remaining dirty set fits the configured downtime target, stops shrinking, or reaches the configured round limit, bhyve pauses the guest and its devices. It then sends the final dirty pages and the existing snapshot state for the vCPUs, kernel state, and emulated devices.

The destination validates the basic VM geometry, receives memory and state, restores it, and reports that it is ready. Only then does the source send GO, the commit point. Before GO, a failed migration can resume the source guest. The destination does not start the guest if it does not receive that commit message. A warm, stop-and-copy mode is available too, which is useful both as a fallback and as a comparison baseline.

What is implemented today Pre-copy and warm migration: live pre-copy is configurable with downtime and maximum-round controls; explicit stop-and-copy migration is also supported. Multi-vCPU protocol support: the migration handshake carries the guest vCPU count, the destination refuses a count mismatch, and all guest vCPUs are paused and resumed as part of migration. The published test bed has primarily exercised a one-vCPU guest, so multi-vCPU stress and race testing remain required before making broader claims. Memory consistency checks: dirty-page tracking covers guest and mapped emulation writes through page dirty state, while vmm write holds are recorded separately. The test workload rewrites and verifies guest memory and reports any missing or stale page as a mismatch. Repeated ping-pong migrations have been used to check that the workload continues without errors. Disk-write validation: a guest-side workload repeatedly writes and fsyncs files, verifies checksums, and is checked again after a cold reboot. This is intended to exercise the device pause, drain, and restore path. Failure handling: destination refusal, an unreachable target, and a target disappearing during both pre-copy and stop-and-copy have been tested. Before commit, the source is intended to resume the paused guest after failure. Basic destination checks: protocol version, page size, memory layout, and vCPU count are checked before data transfer. The migration socket is opened by bhyvectl and passed into bhyve so that bhyve can remain inside its Capsicum sandbox. Supported scope: this is amd64-only and depends on the experimental BHYVE_SNAPSHOT support. It relies on snapshot-capable emulated devices; PCI passthrough is not migratablem, yet. Observed results

In the current two-host test environment, repeated live migrations, memory-rewrite workloads, and fsync-heavy disk workloads have completed successfully. For a slowly dirtying 512 MiB guest, observed downtime has been roughly 138–171 ms. A rapidly dirtying guest may not converge during pre-copy, but still falls back to a correct stop-and-copy completion with a longer pause. These are encouraging engineering results, not a production support promise or a complete correctness proof.

Blockers before upstreaming can be evaluated further

The following are neutral engineering requirements, not criticism of the value of the prototype. They need to be addressed first before further upstreaming into FreeBSD can be evaluated responsibly.

Prove and harden dirty-log correctness. The kernel-side dirty-page algorithm must be demonstrated not to lose a write while dirty bits are examined and cleared. It needs focused concurrency, paging, emulation-write, and multi-vCPU stress coverage, plus a reviewable locking and memory-ordering argument. Define a complete compatibility contract. Matching memory size and vCPU count is not enough. A destination should verify guest identity, CPU capabilities, bhyve/vmm and snapshot format compatibility, device topology and capabilities, and shared-storage identity before accepting a migration. Harden the transport and protocol. The current TCP transport has no authentication or encryption and uses a first-version native protocol. A stable protocol needs explicit wire formats, bounded message handling, timeouts, version negotiation, authentication or a supported external secure transport model, and clear operational guidance. Clarify the commit and device-side-effect boundary. The source/destination handoff must be reviewed so that device restoration cannot cause externally visible work before the source has committed, and so that the unavoidable uncertain outcome after a lost post-commit acknowledgement is operationally recoverable. Specify storage and network handoff. Shared storage must have defined coherency, durability, and fencing assumptions. Network migration also needs a clear answer for tap/bridge handling, MAC/IP movement, and traffic convergence. Build an in-tree test strategy. The current scripts and test-bed workloads are useful, but upstream review will need automated regression coverage and a documented support matrix across CPU counts, memory sizes, supported devices, host CPUs, and failure cases. Separate the work into reviewable patches. Dirty-page tracking, snapshot API refactoring, protocol/receiver work, CLI changes, and tests should be independently reviewable. This will make design feedback more actionable and reduce the risk of merging coupled changes. Next steps

We have already had deeper discussions about these questions in the Sylve Discord. Publishing this current state is intended to make those discussions more concrete, bring in wider FreeBSD and bhyve feedback, and turn the prototype into a clear roadmap. The immediate focus is correctness, compatibility validation, transport safety, and repeatable tests—not adding performance features first. Currently, some peopel already have access to it and it's planned ot publish this at least as a proposal on my git and GitHub at:

git.gyptazy.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration github.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration

Compression, zero-page elision, broader device coverage, richer orchestration, and performance tuning can follow once the foundation is sound. If you operate bhyve, work on FreeBSD virtualisation, or are interested in Sylve or BoxyBSD, testing the RFC and contributing design feedback would be especially valuable.

Status: WIP RFC for a first working bhyve live-migration implementation on FreeBSD 15.1.

entry.title: FAA issues national ground stop
entry.content:
U.S. air traffic experienced a near halt on Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights that lasted more than five hours.

The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET, after thousands of flights were cancelled and airports across the country became packed with stranded, irritated passengers.

The unexpected and highly unusual alert was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” The alert contained no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”

Follow along for live coverage.

“Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis,” the FAA had said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a White House news conference Friday evening that the ground stop was sparked by “instability for our radar and our communications in our centers, in our TRACONS throughout the country.”

TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control, and is an air traffic control center.

That instability was detected at 3:36 p.m., he said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a cyberattack and the public was never in danger.

“There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night.

Earlier Friday, Mullin said the ground stop was the result of a telecommunications outage “as of now.”

When the FAA issued the alert, 4,042 flights headed for U.S. destinations were airborne, according to Flightradar24, a Swedish service that displays real-time aircraft flight tracking information.

Mullin said President Donald Trump has been briefed and that they “are not ruling out anything at this point” in terms of what caused the communications issue. He said those currently on flights have no reason for concern. “We are assured that everybody is safe,” he said.

While the investigation into the failure is in a very early stage, there is no indication that the incident has been caused by malicious activity, officials from multiple agencies that are involved in the situation told NBC News.

They said they haven’t seen the type of activity that would normally be associated with a cyberattack. The officials, however, cautioned that the assessment could change as investigators learn more.

Three senior officials said there’s nothing that indicates a connection between Friday’s incident with the FAA’s systems and the Microsoft outage the day before.

Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.

“Daily we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”

But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, was at capacity, and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, meaning there was no place for the planes to park, a source with knowledge told NBC News.

FOR SUBSCRIBERSBlue wave ignites a wild, wide-open 2028 race FOR SUBSCRIBERSIn China, Nvidia scandal stirs defiance and skepticism FOR SUBSCRIBERSBlue wave ignites a wild, wide-open 2028 race FOR SUBSCRIBERSIn China, Nvidia scandal stirs defiance and skepticism

With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.

Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary” and said he doesn’t know what would have caused it.

Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.

He added that the situation is turning from a safety issue to a massive logistics problem. Airports are becoming crowded with planes trying to land as the aircraft currently on the ground aren’t able to depart. Planes on the ground may have to move and park on taxiways, Guzzetti said.

There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage.

At Newark Liberty International Airport, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed.

“I’m as much in the dark as everyone else. I’m not getting any information from anybody,” one controller at Newark said, according to the feed.

Shortly before the FAA issued its alert, both major airports in Chicago — O’Hare and Midway International Airport — were listed on a ground stop alert due to an “equipment outage,” NBC Chicago reported.

Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”

Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement.

“Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now, our plane is heading back to the terminal, so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.”

United Airlines issued a statement acknowledging the ground stop. “United flights that are already airborne will continue,” the statement said. “New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place.”

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.

In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

entry.title: Lying to Zed to get its remote server running on FreeBSD
entry.content:
I’ve used VS Code since I was about 16, so for almost ten years and honestly it was mostly fine. But as of late it has become unbearable: slow, and increasingly weighed down by AI slop. grahamperrin@ pointed out to me that VS Code now has chat.disableAIFeatures, and they’re right. I totally missed it! It really does turn the built-in AI features off atleast from what I can see in limited testing, and it works. But even with it off, VS Code still feels clunky as hell. Zed, on the other hand, is fast, and it had a native switch that turns all of its AI stuff off slightly earlier than VS Code did, which I absolutely adore. (It’s a toggle in Settings, or "disable_ai": true in your settings file.)

That’s not because I avoid LLMs. I just don’t want them trying to edit every line I write, or sitting in the corner judging me ominously. I still write most of my FOSS code myself: it keeps me sane, and I feel FOSS developers have a responsibility to keep code clean for LLMs to steal from lol. What I do hand off is the tiring part: regression testing, edge cases, and exploration beyond what my tiny 20-watt brain can hold. For that I use harnesses that work well with models, like OpenCode. Beyond auto-complete.. I’ve always found entire harnesses like claude code etc. very clunky in editors.

Getting it working

Zed has no FreeBSD remote server offering (yet), but FreeBSD can run Linux binaries in spades, so we use Zed’s Linux one. All you need is a FreeBSD server you can SSH into.

1. Turn on Linux compatibility sudo sysrc linux_enable=YES sudo service linux start sudo pkg install linux_base-rl9 kldstat -m linux64 # should print a module 2. Make Zed pick the Linux server

Zed asks the host what platform it runs. FreeBSD says FreeBSD amd64, there’s no server for that, and Zed gives up. This wrapper says Linux x86_64 to that one question and passes everything else to the real uname. Save it as ~/.local/bin/uname and make it executable:

#!/bin/sh case "$#:$*" in 1:-sm|1:-ms) printf 'Linux x86_64\n' ;; *) exec /usr/bin/uname "$@" ;; esac

Put ~/.local/bin on PATH for non-interactive SSH sessions. For zsh, add this to ~/.zshenv (use your shell’s equivalent):

export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

It’s a small lie, but a contained one, and the part I’d love to retire.

3. Connect.

Connect over SSH from Zed and open a folder. The first connection uploads the Linux server to ~/.zed_server/. To watch, run tail -f ~/.local/share/zed/logs/server-workspace-*.log.

4. Run a kernel with the (FreeBSD) fix

Without it you’ll connect fine and get an empty project tree, with this in the server log:

error processing entry failed to read directory entry Caused by: Invalid argument (os error 22)

The fix is ec6629628cb, in main, stable/15 and releng/15.2, so 15.2-RELEASE will include it. If the error persists, check you booted the new kernel with uname -v.

The bug in layman terms

To show your project, Zed asks the server for the names of the files in each folder, a few at a time. Zed sets aside a small amount of space for each batch.

Picture a teacher reading a class roll to a student who writes the names on a sticky note (I couldn’t come up with a better analogy, bare with me). The teacher crosses off each name as she reads it, and she never reads a crossed-off name again. The student’s note has room for 6 names. The teacher reads in groups of 4, a sensible habit that works fine almost every time. But 6 isn’t a whole number of groups, so she reads 8 names and crosses all 8 off. Only 6 fit on the note.

Now she’s in a bind. Her slip was grabbing more than fit before checking. She can’t hand over the 6 that fit and keep the other 2 for later, because they’re already crossed off and she would never read them again. So she reports an error instead, which at least is loud. When I tried the quiet way, 112 of my 1,002 files vanished (from the listing) with no warning. A loud error beats a quiet loss I’m pretty sure. Zed saw the error and decided it couldn’t read the folder, and showed it up empty.

The fix is small: read no more names than fit on the note. Read 6, cross off 6, come back for the next 6, until the roll is done. In the real bug, the teacher is FreeBSD’s Linux translator (Linuxulator), the note is a 768-byte buffer, and a group of 4 names is a 512-byte block.

For the kernel nerds

This is a regression. A February 2026 fix for NFS directories returning bogus entries (110f2567cb51, PR 292282) changed how sys/compat/linux/linux_file.c sizes its native read, in both linux_getdents() and linux_getdents64():

/* before February 2026 */ buflen = min(args->count, MAXBSIZE); /* after: every request rounded up to a 512-byte block */ buflen = min(roundup2(args->count, DEV_BSIZE), MAXBSIZE);

If the caller’s buffer isn’t a multiple of 512 bytes, the native batch can outgrow it. The emulation layer converts records until one doesn’t fit and returns EINVAL, but kern_getdirentries() has already advanced the directory offset past the whole batch. That’s why returning a partial batch isn’t enough on its own.

The fix (ec6629628cb, reviewed in D60760):

if (args->count >= DEV_BSIZE) buflen = min(args->count, MAXBSIZE); else buflen = roundup2(args->count, DEV_BSIZE);

It’s safe because Linux directory records are never larger than FreeBSD’s: for dirent64 the header is 19 bytes against 24, and both round each record up to a multiple of 8. A native batch that fits in the caller’s buffer translates into one that fits too.

Legacy getdents had the same bug for 32-bit and 64-bit callers. My first patch only fixed getdents64; fixing both took the test matrix from 86 failures to zero.

Acknowledgements

I’ve had plenty of patches merged before this one, but this was among the quickest to land in releng/15.2: it didn’t sit in stable for long (thankfully!). The release engineering team (re@) runs a really cool process that I am yet to fully understand in depth. Thank you also to Kyle Evans (kevans@) and Mark Johnston (markj@) for reviewing the patch and for their notes along the way.

entry.title: How Not to Build a Music Player
entry.content:
The Twelve-Day War made me realize online music players aren’t a viable option for those who live under an oppressive regime that disconnects the internet across the country as a way to silence public opinion.

So, as soon as the connection came back, I started archiving tracks and looking for offline alternatives and discovered Strawberry. It’s a feature-rich music player and kept me happy for quite a while, but I have this habit of looking at song lyrics and singing along! Strawberry fetches lyrics from the internet when it recognizes a song, but sometimes the lyrics weren’t line-synced and worse, it displayed the timestamps next to the lyrics which I found pretty annoying to look at. I wasn’t aware of other music players such as foobar2000 which my friend just pointed me to while writing this post.

I decided to write my own music player and call it AMP with a few goals in mind: minimal feature-set, no C++ dependencies, proper system integration to make it feel like a native app, and of course, write it in Zig (including the shaders!). I also wanted to roll my own UI because of the fun memories of working on V’s UI during my first days of being introduced into system programming. But before I could make any meaningful progress, a new wave of protests started. Following the tragedy of January 8 and 9, another internet blackout began, lasting more than four months.

During the blackout, there were these anonymous people on Telegram selling internet access through personal White SIMs, whitelisted servers, Starlink dishes, etc. A black market had formed for the freaking internet! You’d get charged $5 or more for just 1GB of traffic. The prices dropped slightly after a while, but it was still hella expensive. The regime surely made a lot of money out of it. I ended up spending hundreds of dollars on these services and other methods just to stay in touch with my friends and keep my hobbies alive. Killing time was becoming a problem. Especially for someone like me who built their entire social life online.

I carefully used this slow connection to download repositories, documention, etc. to continue working on my music player. It really brought me immense joy during this hard time.

Once the connection was mostly restored to the pre-blackout days (UDP traffic is still blocked, though, which naturally also affects QUIC), my attention was shifted towards LLMs. It had become very hard for me to ignore the hype and progress around frontier LLMs. As I really never thought about using them seriously for coding. They are still everywhere in the news, and I was just reminded that I owned a Claude Max 20x subscription gift from my boss back in 2025. Eating dust and maybe soon expiring. So I decided to give it a try and experiment on my music player. It was a very addictive experience. I literally couldn’t hit the plan limits no matter how hard I tried, so after a few non-stop days of prompting, a good chunk of AMP was vibecoded..

At the time, I thought this was an okay approach for a hobby project and I could just un-slopify it later. Little did I know I’m mentally incapable of reviewing tens of thousands lines of code. Shortly after, Anthropic figured that I live in Iran and instantly banned my account. Then Codeberg announced its no-AI policy, which gave me two choices. Either get rid of all that slop or move the repository elsewhere. Going with the former option, I started reading every single line of code, rewriting them. I was surprised by my own ignorance and how much LLMs like to complicate stuff. (I wish I could show an example, but my memory is extremely fragile and I’ve got no pre-rewrite history of the repo to check).

Four months later, nearly half the codebase is gone, and somehow it’s more robust with the same set of features (and more). I regret relying on LLMs in the first place, but hey, lesson learned. That said I think it’s still possible to create a healthy relationship with LLMs as long as you look at them as a fancy IDE feature. A lot of times they are just running long sed or regex commands that are a no-brainer act for humans when done by hand but still consumes a good time. For now and hopefully forever I think I’ll be going the old school way. Never rush your hobbies!

Btw this is how AMP looks like right now!

entry.title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
entry.content:
Terminal borders that don't cost a cell

This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.

I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.

Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough ┌──┐ by hand to have opinions about this.

The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:

So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.

Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.

Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:

Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.

What I'd use it for Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side. Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top. Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge. Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text. Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it. Up close

The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:

The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:

Charts

Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:

And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines:

In motion

Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:

Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:

What box characters can't do

The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.

Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.

You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.

Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little │ cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways.

How it works

A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.

The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters (▖▗▘▝ and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time.

The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.

Styles and joints

Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.

When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher priority wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.

The wire format

Everything is one DCS string with a namespace:

ESC P 1 + b cell-border ; OP ; FIELDS... ESC \

The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:

ESC P 1 + b cell-border;pen;48;32;7aa2f7;0;0 ESC \ bottom edge, blue: an underline hello ESC [ 0 m SGR 0 clears the pen

There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a cell-border reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS.

The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.

Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.

The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the 1 in DCS 1 + b). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.

Prior art

Parts of this have been done before:

DEC ruled lines in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color. SGR 51 to 65: framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge. The Win32 console has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. PDCurses and X/Open curses (WA_TOP, WA_LEFT and friends) have similar attributes. These are the closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves. IBM 3270 terminals can outline whole input fields.

What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.

My own first prototype was in Rio (raphamorim/rio#1947), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.

The awkward (edge) cases

When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.

Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.

Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.

Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.

On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.

Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.

Try it

The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):

git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ghostty.git cd ghostty zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dxcframework-target=native open zig-out/Ghostty.app

Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:

python3 scripts/cell-borders.py # the default view python3 scripts/cell-borders.py --styles # line styles, joints and outside fill

Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: p placement, c colors, h blocks, j junctions, e halves, s styles and l live. w cycles the stroke width, b turns borders off so you can compare, and q quits. Each view also has a matching flag (--placement, --styles and so on) if you want to start on it.

The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:

git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ratatui.git cd ratatui cargo run -p tiling-panes

Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. n and v split, x closes, and right click opens a pane menu. Press b to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or g to shade alternate cells and see where the edges are.

The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:

To run it:

cargo run -p cell-border-top

It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. 1 to 4 show and hide the boxes, b and g work the same as in the panes demo, and h or ? lists the rest of the keys. It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the sysinfo dependency.

What I'd like to hear

I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.
